source.title_on_document: StoryScope: Investigating idiosyncrasies in AI fiction

supplement.where: Appendices A to I are in this PDF (pp. 17-30). Code, the 10,272 writing prompts, and the 51,336 AI-generated stories are at https://github.com/jenna-russell/storyscope (p. 1, footnote 1). The human-written stories are not released (p. 3, footnote 4).
supplement.holds: Corpus statistics (Tables 4-5, p. 17); feature taxonomy (Table 6, p. 19); human validation of the feature assignment (Table 7, p. 19); memorization audit (Tables 8-9, pp. 21-22); per-class F1 (Table 11, p. 21); length audit (Table 10, p. 22); per-story rarity analysis with SDs, AUC, and Cohen's d (Appendix G, p. 22; Table 12 and Figure 5, p. 23); core and fingerprint feature lists (Tables 13, 14, and 16, pp. 24, 25, 27); human and AI means for the core features (Table 15, p. 26); prompts (Figures 6-8, pp. 28-30).

paper_design_summary: The authors extract 10,272 published human-written stories from Books3 anthologies, reverse-engineer a writing prompt from each with Gemini 2.5 Flash, and have five LLMs (Gemini 3 Flash, Kimi K2.5, DeepSeek V3.2, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4) generate stories, yielding a corpus of 61,608 stories (p. 3, Section 2 and footnote 8; p. 17, Tables 4-5). Gemini 3 Flash assigns 304 features to each story for classification, and the authors compare human and AI stories on rarity and dispersion in the encoded narrative-feature space (p. 5, Section 2.2; p. 9, Section 5; p. 22, Appendix G). No person produces creative output with AI assistance; the human stories are existing published works (p. 3, Section 2 and footnote 6).

studies.label: Parallel corpus: Books3 human stories vs stories by five LLMs from the same prompts

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing is assigned to people. The prompt reverse-engineered from each human story goes to five LLMs. The human story and the five AI stories form the six sources.
assignment.quote: We extract 10,272 human-written stories from Books3 (Presser, 2020). To generate mirrored AI stories, we reverse-engineer writing prompts from each human story by prompting Gemini 2.5 Flash

arms.name: Human
arms.description: 10,272 human-written short stories extracted from short story anthologies in Books3, one per prompt (p. 3; Table 4, p. 17).

arms.name: AI (five LLMs)
arms.description: Stories written from the reverse-engineered prompts by Gemini 3 Flash (10,261), GPT-5.4 (10,272), Claude Sonnet 4.6 (10,259), DeepSeek V3.2 (10,272), and Kimi K2.5 (10,272): 51,336 in total (Table 5, p. 17). The creativity-related contrasts pool the five models.

participants.exclusions: No human creative-task participants were analyzed. The corpus contains 61,608 stories (10,272 human, 51,336 AI); models refused to generate 24 stories (p. 3, footnote 8; p. 17, Tables 4-5). Classifiers train on 52,707 stories (8,788 prompts) and test on 8,301 stories (1,384 prompts) (p. 5, Section 3; p. 20, Appendix D). In the rarity analysis, 1,377 human and 6,885 AI test stories were analyzed, 8,262 in total (p. 22, Appendix G; p. 23, Table 12). The paper does not explain the difference between the classifier test count and the rarity sample. A memorization audit flags 169 of 10,139 audited prompts as high risk; the rerun excluding those prompts reports classification outcomes only (p. 21, Appendix E; p. 22, Table 9). Two annotators checked feature coding on 12 existing stories and produced no creative output (p. 19, Appendix C and Table 7).
participants.who: No study participants. The human side is published short stories extracted from anthologies in Books3 (p. 3, footnote 6; p. 28, Figure 6). The paper does not count or describe their authors, so the population code is nominal. The AI side is five LLMs.
participants.quote: We apply STORYSCOPE to a parallel corpus of 10,272 writing prompts, each written by a human author and five LLMs (Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini , GPT, and Kimi), yielding 61,608 stories
participants.locator: p. 1, Abstract; p. 3, Section 2, Data and footnote 6; p. 17, Tables 4-5

ai_tool.name_model: Story generation: Gemini 3 Flash, Kimi K2.5, DeepSeek V3.2, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4. Pipeline: Gemini 2.5 Flash (prompt extraction), GPT-5.1 (templates, comparative analysis, feature discovery), Gemini 3 Flash with minimal thinking (feature assignment).
ai_tool.how_used: The LLMs write complete stories on their own from the reverse-engineered prompts (mean 4,753 words across the corpus, p. 3, footnote 8). No person uses the AI.

task.description: Short-story writing from a prompt reverse-engineered from a published story. The prompt names the story's key characters or setting, conveys its theme, and sets a target length ('approximately N words').
task.duration: Not applicable (no participants; the AI stories are model generations).

outcomes.name: Per-story narrative rarity percentile
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Rarity is the mean Euclidean distance from a story to its k = 25 nearest neighbors in the pooled train+val narrative-feature space, expressed as a percentile of the train+val rarity distribution (p. 22). The vectors encode the narrative features that Gemini 3 Flash assigns to each story; they are not a neural text embedding. The paper uses rarity as a proxy for originality (p. 2). Effect sizes are computed over individual test-set stories. Variants: the share of stories in the top 1, 5, and 10 percent rarest (Table 12) and the share of prompts where the human story is the rarest of the six versions. Human test stories are longer than AI test stories (mean 6,418 vs 4,523 words, p. 21), and rarity is not reported on the length-matched subset.

contrasts.reported: Mean rarity percentile Human 0.71 vs AI 0.49 (AUC = 0.73); sample SDs 0.227 (human) and 0.274 (pooled AI), pooled SD 0.267; n = 1,377 human and 6,885 AI test stories; Cohen's d = 0.83. Top 10% rarest: 24.7% of human vs 7.1% of AI stories; top 1%: 3.0% vs 0.6%. The human story is the rarest of the six versions for 57.8% of prompts (vs 16.7% by chance; mean margin = 0.96 raw distance units). Table 12 counts out of 1,377 per source (Human, Claude, GPT, DeepSeek, Kimi, Gemini): top 1%: 42, 5, 5, 11, 6, 14; top 5%: 180, 33, 34, 58, 64, 45; top 10%: 340, 66, 71, 127, 135, 88.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Section 5, 'Human narratives are rarer'; p. 22, Appendix G; p. 23, Table 12 and Figure 5

outcomes.name: Dispersion of stories in narrative-feature space (mean distance to own-source centroid; median 10-nearest-neighbor radius)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Euclidean distances in the z-scored encoded narrative-feature space. The vectors encode LLM-assigned narrative features (Gemini 3 Flash), not a neural text embedding; embedding_similarity is the closest code. Two statistics: the mean distance of a source's stories to that source's centroid (its radius) and the median 10-nearest-neighbor radius. Related separation statistics on the same page: mean human-AI centroid distance 6.6 vs mean AI-AI centroid distance 4.3 (printed as 1.6x); closest human-AI centroid pair 6.2 vs most distant AI-AI pair 6.0. Figure 2 (p. 7) shows an LDA projection in which the five AI models cluster together.

contrasts.reported: Human stories' mean distance to the human centroid is 22% greater than the average AI radius (33.2 vs. 27.4); their median 10-nearest-neighbor radius is 1.13x larger (33.1 vs. 29.2). No standard errors, intervals, or tests.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Section 5, 'AI convergence separates from human narratives' (paragraph starts on p. 8); p. 7, Figure 2

diversity_detail.metric: Mean Euclidean distance of a source's stories to that source's centroid (radius); median 10-nearest-neighbor radius. Higher values mean more dispersed, so no sign reversal is needed.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: None. The vectors are z-scored encodings of the narrative features that Gemini 3 Flash assigns to each story.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each story against the centroid of its own source. The human value is the mean over human stories. The AI value is printed as 'the average AI radius'; the paper does not define it, but it reports per-model centroids on the same page. The pool that supplies the 10 nearest neighbors is not stated.
diversity_detail.notes: The paper calls these group-level statistics (p. 22) and prints one value per side. It does not state which split (full corpus, train+val, or test) or which feature subset enters the calculation; the surrounding text discusses the narrative-only 6-way classifier. Human stories come from many authors, while each AI source is one model.

outcomes.name: Core narrative-feature levels, human vs AI (30 core features, Table 15)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Per-story narrative features assigned by Gemini 3 Flash: 1-5 Likert scales (means), ordinal codes (means over integer codes), or the prevalence of one categorical or binary option (percent). The 30 core features fill 33 feature-option rows, 20 AI-elevated and 13 human-elevated, because three features appear once on each side (Subplot Integration, Reference Explicitness, Emotional Expression). The paper selects them because they separate human from AI stories in the binary classifier (p. 5; p. 20). One group is labeled 'Human-elevated: Narrative diversity' (location variety, dialogue share, thematically parallel subplots, morally ambivalent protagonists, explicit emotion labels). It describes variety within a story, not diversity across people's outputs, so the construct is other. This is a descriptive outcome, not a creativity score. Gap = Human minus AI. A few printed gaps differ by one in the last digit from the difference of the printed columns (e.g., 42% vs 21%, gap +22). Which stories enter the means is not stated.

contrasts.reported: Human vs AI (Gap = Human - AI; the AI column averages across all five models). AI-elevated examples: Thematic Explicitness & Moralizing 3.28 vs 3.94 (-0.65); Narratorial Thematic Commentary -> yes 52% vs 77% (-25); Emotional Expression -> embodied 38% vs 81% (-42). Human-elevated: Narrative diversity: Location Variety Scope 1.34 vs 1.08 (+0.26); Dialogue-to-Narration Proportion 2.95 vs 2.70 (+0.24); Subplot Integration -> thematically parallel 42% vs 21% (+22); Moral Polarity -> ambivalent/mixed 59% vs 38% (+21); Emotional Expression -> explicit labels 29% vs 8% (+21). No standard deviations, standard errors, or tests.
contrasts.locator: p. 26, Table 15; p. 7, Section 4.1; p. 22, Appendix H

eligibility.reason: This is an AI-versus-human corpus comparison, not a study assigning people to AI assistance. Published Books3 stories are paired with stories generated by five LLMs from reverse-engineered prompts (p. 3, Section 2). Random selection of discovery prompts and random ordering of templates in LLM-facing comparisons do not assign people to AI conditions (p. 4, Section 2.1; p. 17, Appendix B), so criterion 1 is not met. No human creative-task participants were analyzed; the corpus and rarity sample counts are stories, not people (p. 17, Tables 4-5; pp. 22-23, Appendix G and Table 12). The two human annotators evaluate existing stories and produce no creative output (p. 19, Appendix C), so criterion 2 is not met. Rarity and dispersion are computed on story outputs (p. 9, Section 5; p. 22, Appendix G), which justifies scored_on_output=true for those outcomes and ai_vs_human context inclusion. Criterion 3 nevertheless is not met under the codebook requirement for output that study participants produce: the scored texts here are archival human stories and model generations. The unresolved story-count and dispersion-method details do not affect these eligibility decisions.

one_line_finding: Human-written Books3 stories are rarer in LLM-coded narrative-feature space than stories five LLMs wrote from the same prompts (mean rarity percentile 0.71 vs 0.49, Cohen's d = 0.83; p. 9 and p. 22, Appendix G) and more dispersed around their source centroid (mean distance 33.2 vs average AI radius 27.4; p. 9).
open_questions: Test-set size: pp. 5 and 20 give 1,384 prompts and 8,301 stories, but the rarity analysis and Table 12 use 8,262 test stories (1,377 per source, pp. 22-23), and the length-matched subset also has 1,377 human stories (p. 21). The paper does not explain the gap.
Dispersion (S1-O2): the paper does not state which split or feature subset it uses, which pool supplies the 10 nearest neighbors, or how the 'average AI radius' is formed.
The codebook has no measure code for distances on LLM-coded feature vectors. This form uses automated_score for per-story rarity (S1-O1) and embedding_similarity for dispersion (S1-O2).
Whether the rarity and dispersion results belong in the ai_vs_human context set, given that the paper's main aim is AI detection and authorship attribution.
notes: Most of the paper reports detection and attribution accuracy. These are not creativity or diversity outcomes and are not listed: binary human vs AI macro-F1 93.2% narrative-only and 96.0% narrative+style (Table 2, p. 6); six-way attribution macro-F1 68.4% and 77.3% (Table 3, p. 8); 278 LAMP-edited Gemini stories detected at 93.9% macro-F1 (p. 8). The per-source fingerprint features (Table 16, p. 27) report classifier SHAP importance and uniqueness ratios, rather than creativity or diversity outcome contrasts, and are not listed. The percentages and ratios on p. 9 are retained as printed, without recalculating them from rounded values. Page 9 calls the top-10-percent tail 'corpus-wide', while Appendix G and Table 12 describe the tails on the test set. Final review covered the complete markdown conversion, including Appendices A-I, and checked the recorded outcome statistics and eligibility evidence against the PDF. No c021 challenge files were present; the final resolution counters count challenge problems. The reconciliation object is unchanged. All original open questions are assessed in final.open_items; the measure-code and context-inclusion questions need no further source material.

differences.resolved: embedding_similarity. The outcome is Euclidean distances between story vectors in a z-scored encoded feature space. The vectors are LLM-coded narrative features rather than a neural text embedding, which measure_detail states. Among the allowed codes, embedding_similarity (distances between vector representations of the texts) fits best.

open_items.item: Test-set size (open_questions[0]): the classifier test set has 1,384 prompts and 8,301 stories (pp. 5 and 20), whereas the rarity analysis has 8,262 stories, 1,377 per source (pp. 22-23); the length-matched analysis also uses 1,377 human stories (p. 21). Matching story IDs and filtering steps in the posted data/code would settle the discrepancy. This concerns output counts and cannot establish a sample of human creative-task participants for criterion 2.

Dispersion methods (open_questions[1]): the split, feature subset, 10-nearest-neighbor reference pool, and aggregation underlying the average AI radius are not specified for the p. 9 statistics. The posted analysis code and its input data would settle these details. They affect reproducibility of context results, not any core eligibility criterion.

Measure coding (open_questions[2]): resolved for screening by retaining automated_score for per-story rarity and embedding_similarity as the closest available code for dispersion, with explicit notes that the vectors encode LLM-assigned narrative features rather than neural text embeddings (pp. 5, 9 and 22). This vocabulary choice does not change any eligibility criterion.

Context inclusion (open_questions[3]): resolved as ai_vs_human under codebook Section 3. The paper explicitly uses rarity as a proxy for originality (p. 2) and reports story rarity and dispersion (p. 9; pp. 22-23), so these results qualify as context despite the main focus on detection and attribution. This does not make the study eligible for the core dataset.
